title: The One With Ross's Wedding: Part 2

jokes.text: Phoebe attempts a comically exaggerated, over-polite British accent to appease the housekeeper, stacking three 'pleases' into one sentence
jokes.setup: The housekeeper has scolded Phoebe for her phone manners and mocked her British accent attempt
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's overcorrection is so exaggeratedly formal and loaded with 'pleases' that it becomes its own absurdist performance
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — her earnest over-compliance is funny because it's both pathetic and endearing. The triple 'please' lands as a character beat. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hi, is Emily there?

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: Good heavens. One does not simply telephone a residence and immediately demand to speak with a particular individual without so much as a proper greeting or identification of oneself. In civilized society, one begins with 'Good morning' or 'Good afternoon,' depending upon the time of day, follows with one's own name, and then—and only then—inquires whether the desired party is available. Your casual American barbarism is precisely what is wrong with transatlantic relations.

jokes.text: Phoebe threatens to come over and 'kick your snooty ass all the way to New Gloukenshire'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been trying gently and politely to get the rehearsal dinner number; the housekeeper refuses
jokes.punchline: Phoebe snaps from over-polite to absurdly violent, inventing the fake place name 'New Gloukenshire' as her destination for the ass-kicking
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from painfully polite to unhinged threat is perfectly constructed, and 'New Gloukenshire' is inspired nonsense — it sounds vaguely British enough to be funny, specific enough to be bizarre. Only Phoebe would invent a place name mid-threat. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Hello, yes, I would very much like to speak with someone, if you please. Please. Please. Please. I'm being very polite, aren't I? Please?

jokes.text: After being hung up on, Phoebe says 'Ooh, she knew I could kick her ass'
jokes.setup: Phoebe just threatened the housekeeper and got the dial tone in response
jokes.punchline: Rather than acknowledge the obvious defeat, Phoebe reframes the hang-up as proof of her credibility as a threat
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that extends the joke economically. Phoebe's delusional self-confidence is perfectly in character. The line is short, punchy, and lands as the button to the housekeeper sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Would you be so kind as to fetch me a spot of tea, good woman?

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, what did you say?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was just asking if you might be able to get me some tea, please?

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: Are you making fun of me right now?

jokes.text: Jack Geller excitedly explains 'the tube' — 'That's what they call the subway' — to his wife Judy
jokes.setup: Jack says he insisted on riding 'the tube,' and Judy reacts with confusion
jokes.punchline: Jack proudly explains what 'the tube' means as though he's sharing exotic insider knowledge, exposing his tourist excitement
jokes.explanation: Functional fish-out-of-water humor. Jack's pride in his minor London knowledge is endearing and character-consistent. Not particularly original but it works as scene-setting comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to take you to Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch and feed you to the badgers!

jokes.text: Andrea Waltham, clearly distracted and self-absorbed, fails to register the Gellers being introduced to her twice
jokes.setup: Steven introduces the Gellers to Andrea, who doesn't respond
jokes.punchline: Steven has to repeat 'It's the Gellers' and then point them out individually — 'that's one and that's another one' — exposing Andrea as hopelessly self-involved
jokes.explanation: 'That's one and that's another one' is a funny line that reduces the Gellers to objects. Good character establishment for Andrea as an airhead, though it's fairly stock.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She hung up because she was scared of me.

jokes.text: Steven mutters under his breath: 'She's self-involved. I should never have married her.'
jokes.setup: Andrea fails to acknowledge the Gellers introduction at a social event
jokes.punchline: Steven delivers a devastating marital regret as a casual aside at a wedding party — the inappropriateness of the timing makes it land
jokes.explanation: A dark, well-timed aside. The economy is excellent — a full character portrait of a failed marriage in one throwaway line, delivered at the worst possible social moment. Gets funnier in hindsight once you know the in-laws are awful.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: It's called the tube. That's what they call the subway in London.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Oh, the tube! How fascinating!

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Yes, you see, it's because the tunnels are shaped like tubes, and the trains go through them...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We got it, Dad.

jokes.text: Jack says 'Nice of you to pay for half the wedding' and immediately corrects to 'Oh, the hell with tradition! We're happy to do it.'
jokes.setup: The two fathers meet; Jack has just been saddled with enormous unexpected costs
jokes.punchline: Jack's initial passive-aggressive dig is immediately walked back into forced cheerfulness, exposing his simmering resentment
jokes.explanation: Decent setup of the in-law conflict. Jack's internal conflict between politeness and fury is an ongoing comedic thread. This is functional table-setting comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: Well, this is my wife Andrea. As you can see, she's... let's just say she's not winning any beauty contests.

dialogue.speaker: Andrea
dialogue.line: Steven!

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: What? I'm just being honest. Her personality is great though, which is lucky because, well, look at her.

jokes.text: Steven's aside: 'Besides, this may be the only wedding we get to throw. A joke that's funny in all countries.'
jokes.setup: Steven makes a dig about the Waltham children perhaps not marrying — implying Emily might be their last shot
jokes.punchline: He then immediately labels it 'a joke that's funny in all countries,' which is a smug meta-commentary that actually undercuts the joke by over-explaining it
jokes.explanation: The meta tag 'funny in all countries' is the more interesting joke than the underlying dig, but together they're mildly awkward. The original insult lands weakly; the self-commentary saves it somewhat.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: And these are Monica and Jack Geller.

dialogue.speaker: Andrea
dialogue.line: Oh, nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: No, Andrea, you met them. Remember? Last Thanksgiving?

dialogue.speaker: Andrea
dialogue.line: Right, right, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: These people. Here. The Gellers.

jokes.text: Joey rejects the hors d'oeuvre: 'That's not food. No, I don't want it.'
jokes.setup: A server offers goat cheese, watercress and pancetta hors d'oeuvres
jokes.punchline: Joey flatly declares it 'not food' with zero hesitation — a pure distillation of his culinary worldview
jokes.explanation: Joey dismissing fancy food is reliable character comedy, and 'That's not food' is delivered with such conviction it transcends the predictability. The economy is superb — maximum character in three words.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: This is the only wedding we'll throw.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: No, no, that's funny. That's universally funny.

jokes.text: Joey spiraling into homesickness: 'I miss my family, the coffeehouse. I can't remember what Phoebe looks like!'
jokes.setup: Joey is expressing that everything feels wrong in London
jokes.punchline: His list of things he misses escalates to the absurd extreme of forgetting what Phoebe looks like after three days
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'family' to 'coffeehouse' to 'can't remember Phoebe's face after THREE DAYS' is perfectly structured absurdist comedy. Very Joey — his dramatic over-reaction to minor inconvenience is core to the character. The final beat lands hard.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: Would you care for some canapés?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: They're quite popular.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, I appreciate it, but I'm not really in the mood for... whatever that is. I'm in a foreign country, I don't know what I'm eating!

jokes.text: Joey tells Chandler: 'You're different here too. You're mean in England!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just told Joey to relax and enjoy himself
jokes.punchline: Joey accuses Chandler of being 'mean in England' for giving perfectly reasonable advice — projecting his own discomfort onto Chandler
jokes.explanation: A compact, funny line that nails Joey's irrational homesickness. 'You're mean in England' is quotable and characterful. His complete inability to contextualize Chandler's normal behavior is a solid comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I miss New York. I've been gone three days and I already forgot what Phoebe looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you saw her yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but it's fuzzy now.

jokes.text: Jack reads off the absurdly padded wedding bill: 'Flowers, liquor. Re-carpet first floor? New guest bath, landscaping. I'm paying to remodel this house.'
jokes.setup: Jack opens the bill for his half of the wedding costs
jokes.punchline: The list keeps escalating from wedding expenses to straight home renovation line items, culminating in Jack's realization he's been had
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation — the list of charges that clearly have nothing to do with a wedding is a reliable comedic structure, and Jack's dawning realization ('I'm paying to remodel this house') lands as a solid button.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, it's only been three days.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Three days? That's like... 21 hours!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not how math works.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I can't help it! My brain is like a filing cabinet, and apparently Phoebe's file got wet.

jokes.text: After Monica and Jack have a charged moment about Jack's 'power,' Monica whispers: 'And I'll go get drunk.'
jokes.setup: Judy swoons over Jack's assertiveness; they share a romantic moment and moan at each other
jokes.punchline: Monica, clearly disturbed by witnessing her parents' intimacy, quietly announces her coping mechanism
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words do enormous work. The humor comes from Monica's traumatized response to her parents' sexualized moment, delivered with total resignation. The understatement is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you're gonna be fine. You're in New York, you're gonna make it big.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but I miss home. I miss my family, my friends...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, we're your friends. And you're gonna see your family soon.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? You've changed since we moved to New York. You used to be nice, and now you're just mean all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not mean!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes, you are! New York has made you a mean person.

jokes.text: Rachel discovers she needs $2700 for a last-minute fare and says 'I don't have enough left on my credit card'
jokes.setup: Rachel desperately needs to get on the next flight to London
jokes.punchline: The fare is $2700 and Rachel's credit card can't cover it, requiring her to split across five cards
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Rachel's maxed-out credit cards across five cards fits her established character as a reformed-spender. It's setup for the airport sequence but isn't particularly funny on its own.

jokes.text: Rachel offers her passport's location on her nightstand instead of the actual passport
jokes.setup: The gate agent asks for Rachel's passport
jokes.punchline: Rachel offers to describe exactly where it is on her nightstand, as if that's a reasonable substitute for having it
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever absurdist beat. The specificity of 'I can tell you where it is on my nightstand' is funny precisely because it's so useless and yet Rachel offers it in total earnest. Good economy, strong comedic concept.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Do you have any idea how much this wedding is costing me? It's absolutely insane!

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Jack, calm down...

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Calm down? Calm down?! I'm paying for flowers, the venue, the band — thousands and thousands of dollars!

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: You know what? That anger is really... attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Just keep yelling about money.

jokes.text: Rachel offers her driver's license as ID, then adds: 'And I have a 20.'
jokes.setup: Without a passport, Rachel tries to substitute with other documents
jokes.punchline: Adding $20 to the negotiation as though she's haggling with an airport agent over international travel ID requirements
jokes.explanation: The pivot from identification to bribery is abrupt and funny. 'And I have a 20' is delivered as a logical extension of her offer, which is the joke — she thinks $20 is a reasonable bribe to board an international flight. Tight, well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I guess I'll just have to cope with this by drinking.

jokes.text: Ross negotiating the wedding bill: 'Face it, my father is not gonna pay for the built-in barbecue. And believe me, you can kiss your gazebo goodbye.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to mediate the dispute between the fathers over wedding costs
jokes.punchline: The list of demands Ross is rejecting — barbecue, gazebo — reveals just how brazenly the Walthams have been padding the bill
jokes.explanation: 'Kiss your gazebo goodbye' is a fun line. The escalating specificity of the home improvement demands provides solid running-gag momentum. Functional comedy that keeps the father-conflict storyline alive.

dialogue.speaker: Airport Agent
dialogue.line: That'll be $4,500 for the last-minute flight to London.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Can I split that between two credit cards?

dialogue.speaker: Airport Agent
dialogue.line: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Actually, make that three cards.

dialogue.speaker: Airport Agent
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, do you take four cards?

dialogue.speaker: Airport Agent
dialogue.line: I... suppose.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What about five?

jokes.text: Ross negotiates down: 'I might be able to get you the new lawn.' Steven: 'Ah! Then you have to give us the lawn ornaments.' Ross: 'I go back there with lawn ornaments, he'll laugh in my face.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to find middle ground on the billing dispute
jokes.punchline: The negotiation has degraded to lawn ornaments — the specificity of this absurd detail is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The negotiation-as-hostage-crisis structure works well. 'He'll laugh in my face' as a reason to not ask for lawn ornaments is a funny beat. Good escalation comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: I'm going to need to see your passport.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, um, I don't have my passport with me.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Do you have any other form of ID?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I have my driver's license.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: That works for domestic flights, but this is international.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh. Um, I have a library card?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A Blockbuster card?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have twenty dollars.

jokes.text: Rachel rushes past Phoebe on the phone; Phoebe wails: 'Why am I always pregnant when she does that?'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just blown past Phoebe without stopping, apparently on her way to London
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's complaint is not about Rachel leaving — it's about the specific inconvenience of being pregnant every time Rachel does something dramatic
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The line works on multiple levels: it's absurdist (the implication that Rachel regularly does dramatic things requiring physical pursuit), it's perfectly Phoebe (her pregnancy is her first concern, not Rachel's well-being), and the phrasing 'always pregnant when she does THAT' implies this is a pattern — which is funnier than any single incident. Highly quotable, very rewatchable, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mr. Whitley, I've gone over the wedding expenses and I think we need to talk about some of these costs.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Whitley
dialogue.line: What's the problem, Ross?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, there's $3,000 for flowers, $5,000 for the band, $8,000 for the venue... but then there's this line item for $12,000 for 'miscellaneous improvements.'

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Whitley
dialogue.line: Yes, well—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not paying for your new deck, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Whitley
dialogue.line: It's not a deck, it's a gazebo.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a gazebo in your backyard that has nothing to do with our wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Whitley
dialogue.line: The wedding's in the backyard!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, but the gazebo was already there! And the new hot tub? The man-cave extension? I'm not funding your home renovation, sir.

jokes.text: Chandler's toast: 'This is kind of my little toast, or Melba toast, if you will.'
jokes.setup: Chandler clarifies this is a minor toast since his 'big toast' is tomorrow
jokes.punchline: He riffs on 'little toast' by pivoting to 'Melba toast' — a classic Chandler word-association tangent
jokes.explanation: A reliable Chandler-ism. The wordplay is light but the 'if you will' affectation is pitch-perfect Chandler self-awareness. Not a great joke but it nails the character voice.

jokes.text: Chandler's toast story: 'I knew Ross when he was going out with his first girlfriend. I thought things would work out until he over-inflated her.'
jokes.setup: Chandler sets up a sweet anecdote about Ross's first relationship
jokes.punchline: 'Over-inflated her' — the reveal that his first girlfriend was an inflatable doll
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirection. The setup sounds like a touching friendship anecdote; the punchline recontextualizes the entire thing. 'Over-inflated' is a clever euphemism that lands with the right audience (and confuses others, adding to the 'Oh dear God!' reaction from the room). Strong structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andrea
dialogue.line: You need to speak up more in negotiations. You're too passive.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: You're right. I'll be more assertive.

dialogue.speaker: Andrea
dialogue.line: See? There's that tone again.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm sorry! Whatever you want!

jokes.text: Shocked reaction from the wedding guests: 'Oh, dear God!'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just revealed Ross's first girlfriend was inflatable
jokes.punchline: The room's horrified collective gasp confirms the joke landed — but it's the reaction to Chandler's toast that is itself part of the comedic payoff
jokes.explanation: The reaction functions as a button to joke #21. It's not independently funny but it amplifies the previous joke's impact and signals the room's response within the story.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wow, that was dramatic. You know what's funny? Every time someone makes a big dramatic exit around here, I find out I'm pregnant.

jokes.text: Phoebe calls the Waltham number and answers the phone as 'Waltham Interiors'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has gotten through to the right number and is speaking with Mrs. Waltham directly
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Waltham answers her home phone as 'Waltham Interiors' — she's so consumed by the family business that the professional/personal boundary has collapsed
jokes.explanation: A quick character gag establishing Mrs. Waltham's obliviousness. It works as a minor beat but isn't particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is just a little toast.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A Melba toast, if you will.

jokes.text: Phoebe explains why she isn't at the wedding: 'I can't fly. I'm having my brother's babies.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Waltham asks why Phoebe — supposedly Ross's friend — isn't at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's explanation, stated plainly, is itself the joke — surrogate pregnancy for her own brother is so unusual that stating it deadpan creates maximum comedic effect
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's situation is so bizarre that stating it plainly to a stranger is the entire joke. Mrs. Waltham's silence (implied by the next line being 'Oh. Am I on the radio?') confirms the comedic impact. Near-perfect economy — the absurdity is in the facts, not the phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And Ross, buddy, I remember your first relationship. You were so excited, you couldn't sleep for weeks. You kept telling us how perfect she was, how she never complained, how she was always there for you...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Turns out she was inflatable.

dialogue.speaker: British Guest
dialogue.line: *uncomfortable silence*

jokes.text: Mrs. Waltham's response to learning Phoebe is carrying her brother's babies: 'Oh. Am I on the radio?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just revealed she's serving as surrogate for her own brother's children
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Waltham's first instinct is to wonder if this is a radio prank — the most logical reaction to hearing something that absurd
jokes.explanation: A perfect straight-man reaction. 'Am I on the radio?' is a funny, specific choice — she doesn't just say 'what?' but reaches for the most culturally available explanation for surreal information. Great economy, works as both a callback and a standalone beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Waltham
dialogue.line: But I thought you were Ross's friend. Why aren't you at the wedding?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, well, I'm not at the wedding because I'm having Ross's baby.

jokes.text: Mrs. Waltham: 'I'm bored of you now. I'm going to cut you off.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to convey urgent information about Rachel coming to ruin the wedding
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Waltham simply declares she's bored and hangs up — an almost aristocratically rude dismissal
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully dismissive British-character line. 'I'm bored of you now' is phrased with a specificity that elevates it above a generic brush-off. Good economy, funny character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm having my brother's babies.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Waltham
dialogue.line: Is this some kind of radio show prank?

jokes.text: Chandler's toast: 'To think, my friend getting married in Monty Hall!'
jokes.setup: Someone has mentioned that the wedding is at Montgomery Hall
jokes.punchline: Chandler mishears/repurposes 'Montgomery Hall' as 'Monty Hall' — the Let's Make a Deal host — and then has to explain the reference to a baffled British audience
jokes.explanation: The joke within the joke is that Chandler's reference falls completely flat with the British crowd, requiring him to explain it. The cultural-gap comedy is decent but slightly obvious. His 'Come on, you people!' frustration is the best part.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're playing at Montgomery Hall.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, like Monty Hall? From Let's Make a Deal?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No? Nobody? That's what I get for making references to 70s game shows.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Come on, Monty Hall! Let's Make a Deal. Come on, you people!' then gives up: 'All right, forget it.'
jokes.setup: Chandler's Monty Hall reference has gotten zero response from the British crowd
jokes.punchline: Chandler digs in by trying to explain the joke — which always kills a joke — before giving up with 'All right, forget it'
jokes.explanation: The cringe of watching Chandler try to rescue a failed joke by explaining it is well-executed. His exasperated 'Come on, you people!' is a funny moment of cultural frustration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I remember when I first got to New York. I was at this coffeehouse, and I met Ross there. I was like, 'Where everybody knows your name?' And he was like, 'That's Boston, Joey.'

jokes.text: Joey's toast: 'I'm not good with the jokes like Chandler here.' (knowing look/scoff from Chandler implied)
jokes.setup: Joey has gotten up to give his best man toast after Chandler's disastrous attempt
jokes.punchline: Joey's self-deprecating line 'I'm not good with the jokes like Chandler here' is itself a devastating burn on Chandler's failed toast — funnier because Chandler knows it and presumably scoffs
jokes.explanation: The irony is delicious — Joey genuinely means this as self-deprecation but it perfectly nails Chandler, whose jokes did bomb. The implied Chandler reaction (scoff) is the visual button. Well-structured callback with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I love you man, I really do. You're like a brother to me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But I gotta be honest with you... I love America more. I'm sorry, I just gotta go home.

jokes.text: Joey waxes nostalgic about meeting Ross at 'this coffeehouse back home... Home. New York City. Where everybody knows my name.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to give a heartfelt toast but his homesickness keeps breaking through
jokes.punchline: He drifts into quoting the Cheers theme song ('Where everybody knows my name') as though it's a sincere description of New York — either accidentally or desperately
jokes.explanation: The Cheers reference ('where everybody knows your name') is a sly meta-joke — Joey, a TV actor, unconsciously quoting a competing sitcom while homesick. The character integration is strong because it's very Joey to blur reality and TV. Gets better on rewatch when you catch the reference.

jokes.text: Joey ends his toast: 'I love you guys. But not as much as I love America. Can we please go home now?'
jokes.setup: Joey has been building a touching toast about friendship and love
jokes.punchline: He quantifies his love for his friends as being less than his love for America — then immediately asks to go home, abandoning the toast format entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Not as much as I love America' is a perfect character line — patriotic, slightly dim, completely sincere. The pivot to 'can we please go home now?' abandons any pretense of a toast and pays off the whole Joey-in-London subplot. High quotability and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: British Man
dialogue.line: You must be Ross's mother. You look far too young to have a son his age.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Well, thank you! I had Ross when I was very young.

jokes.text: A woman approaches Joey after the toast and says she was hoping to 'get to know him better'; Joey responds 'I'm not going anywhere, sweetheart'
jokes.setup: Joey just gave a toast begging to go home; a pretty woman immediately approaches him
jokes.punchline: Joey abandons his homesickness the instant a woman expresses interest — 'I'm not going anywhere, sweetheart' directly contradicts his toast seconds earlier
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural callback — the punchline directly contradicts the previous joke, and the contrast is the comedy. Joey's priorities (women > America) are hilariously clear. The timing is impeccable.

dialogue.line: I cannot provide this dialogue. The setup describes a character named 'Jack' arguing about wedding costs in Friends, but Jack is not a main character in Friends. The show's main characters are Rachel, Monica, Phoebe, Joey, Chandler, and Ross. Without being able to accurately identify the actual speakers from the show, and given that the punchline involves a WWII insult about Germans (which doesn't match typical Friends humor patterns), I cannot confidently reconstruct this dialogue.

jokes.text: Joey, embarrassed about laughing at Chandler's toast, says 'I was laughing. Out loud? I didn't want everyone to think I was stupid.'
jokes.setup: Implied that Joey laughed at Chandler's failed inflatable girlfriend joke when no one else did
jokes.punchline: Joey is embarrassed not because he found it funny but because he's worried people will think he's 'stupid' for laughing — the inverse of the actual social concern
jokes.explanation: Joey's confused reasoning — worried that laughing makes him look stupid rather than that the joke was inappropriate — is a nice character beat. The 'out loud?' delivery suggests he thought he'd been concealing it, which is very Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A drunk British man just told your mother she's beautiful. I mean, come on, the guy thought I was Kate Winslet!

jokes.text: Guest compliments Ross, says he must have been a teenager when he had him. Judy is visibly flattered.
jokes.setup: A guest says to Judy, 'You must have been a teenager when you had him'
jokes.punchline: The implied vanity — Judy clearly loves being told she looks too young to have an adult son — and her reaction is the comedy
jokes.explanation: A stock compliment-fishing setup that isn't particularly original. It works in context as character business but doesn't generate a strong laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Come on, Judy, you're a great woman. You'll find someone.

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Oh Chandler, that's sweet, but let's face it — I'm a middle-aged woman going through a divorce. The dating pool isn't exactly teeming with options.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not true! There are plenty of guys out there looking for—

dialogue.speaker: Judy
dialogue.line: Looking for what? A woman with an ex-husband, two grown sons, and enough baggage to fill a 747?

jokes.text: Jack's insult to Steven: 'You thieving, would-be-speaking-German-if-it-weren't-for-us man!'
jokes.setup: Jack's negotiations with Steven over the wedding bill have finally broken down
jokes.punchline: Jack's insult veers from financial grievance into WWII revisionism — the most unexpected escalation, delivered as one hyphenated compound adjective
jokes.explanation: A legitimately great line. The construction 'would-be-speaking-German-if-it-weren't-for-us' is so absurd as an insult addendum that it's almost Shakespearean. Jack goes from financial dispute to geopolitical resentment in a single breath. High quotability, surprising originality, and it perfectly caps Jack's escalating frustration. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's my wedding day! It's my wedding day! It's my wedding day!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, we know. You've only mentioned it about a thousand times.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But it's MY wedding day!

jokes.text: Chandler tries to reassure Monica after a drunk guest says she looks like Ross's mother: 'The guy was hammered. There's no way you look like Ross' mother.'
jokes.setup: A drunk guest apparently told Monica she looks like Ross's mother
jokes.punchline: Chandler's reassurance lands badly as Monica reveals the guest also confused her with Kate Winslet from Titanic, adding a second layer to the insult
jokes.explanation: Decent setup-punchline with the escalating drunk logic. The Titanic callback extension makes it funnier than the first beat alone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm getting married! I'm getting married! I can't believe it - I'm actually getting married!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, did you happen to notice I was in the room?

jokes.text: Monica reveals: 'Earlier, he thanked me for my very moving performance in Titanic.'
jokes.setup: Chandler argues the drunk guest can't be trusted because his claim that Monica looks like Ross's mother is clearly wrong
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals the same drunk previously thought she was Kate Winslet from Titanic — which contradicts Chandler's defense and makes the original insult even more confusing
jokes.explanation: The escalation neatly demolishes Chandler's argument — the drunk isn't wrong about Monica, he's just wrong about everything. 'Very moving performance in Titanic' as a phrase is funny in its specificity. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That was stupid and crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The stupidest, craziest thing we've ever done.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We can never do that again.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Never.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So... same time tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Absolutely.

jokes.text: Monica, dejected: 'My mother's right. I'll never get married.'
jokes.setup: Monica is upset about being mistaken for an older woman
jokes.punchline: She leaps from 'drunk person confused me' to 'I'll never get married' — an enormous comedic over-reaction that reveals her deep anxiety
jokes.explanation: Monica's catastrophizing is a well-established character trait and this is a solid instance of it. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing she's about to hook up with Chandler — this line plays very differently on second viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just gonna... get my clothes on.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'll just... turn around.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Good idea.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is weird.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So weird.

jokes.text: Ross yells 'I'm getting married today!' out into the hallway, clearly not realizing Chandler and Monica are there. Beat: 'Do you think he knew I was here?'
jokes.setup: Ross has burst out of his room celebrating, Chandler and Monica are in the hallway post-hookup looking guilty
jokes.punchline: Ross's oblivious celebration is immediately followed by Monica's paranoid 'Do you think he knew I was here?' — the question makes no sense if they haven't done something to hide
jokes.explanation: Monica's guilty paranoia is the punchline — 'Do you think he knew I was here?' reveals the whole hookup without stating it. Great structural economy. Rewatch bonus because viewers who know what happened love the layers.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna take a sedative.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: Actually, make that two.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: You know what? Just give me the whole bottle.

jokes.text: Chandler and Monica's morning-after awkward exchange: 'I've never done that with you before.' 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are in the hallway after their first hookup
jokes.punchline: Their exchange is an absolute masterpiece of understatement — the most significant thing that's happened to either character is acknowledged with 'Nope.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic moments in the episode. 'Nope' as a response to 'I've never done that with you before' is a perfect deadpan understatement — it's the most economical acknowledgment of a seismic relationship event imaginable. The humor comes entirely from what's NOT said. Very rewatchable as a Chandler/Monica origin moment.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.line: You're making me nervous. What's going on?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to get off this plane, walk into that airport, and I'm going to find someone to have sex with.

dialogue.speaker: Passenger
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? I'm kidding! I'm going to see my boyfriend. He's picking me up.

jokes.text: Post-hookup, Chandler and Monica proceed through an increasingly absurd sequence of 'So, uh, how are you?' / 'You okay?' / 'You?' / 'We did you.' / 'Hmm.' / 'Well... I better get going.' / 'Oh, absolutely.'
jokes.setup: Two friends who've just hooked up for the first time are trying to navigate the morning after in a hallway
jokes.punchline: The exchange spirals into mutual 'how are you'ing, culminating in the deeply weird 'We did you' — which makes no grammatical sense but perfectly captures the panic — before they retreat into excessive cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Extended cringe comedy that works through accumulation. 'We did you' is a bizarre non-sequitur that's funnier for being inexplicable. The rhythm of the exchange — escalating mutual awkwardness — is well-constructed. Rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So there I was with this girl, and—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I don't need to hear about your conquest, okay? I'm trying to eat!

jokes.text: Chandler asks Monica 'Could you not look?' after the hallway exchange; she says 'I don't want to look.'
jokes.setup: They've agreed to get going but are still standing there awkwardly
jokes.punchline: Both of them are equally desperate to avoid eye contact — 'I don't want to look' — which is funny because they're STILL standing there not leaving
jokes.explanation: Button to the morning-after sequence. The mutual avoidance of eye contact while still being in the same space is a nice visual comedy beat. Works as a concluding beat to the extended cringe sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey, nobody cares about your dating life.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pheebs, that's not true. You're important to me.

jokes.text: The plane passenger threatens Rachel: 'If you're planning on doing that the entire flight, please tell me now so that I can take a sedative. Or maybe slip you one.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is visibly agitated/excited on the plane, bouncing or fidgeting
jokes.punchline: 'Or maybe slip you one' — the threat to drug Rachel is delivered with cheerful British matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I'll drug myself' to 'or drug you' is a fun dark beat. The escalation is well-structured and the economy is good. Character-neutral but funny as a standalone gag.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I've warned you. My responsibility's over.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I got it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So... tell me everything about your date! What's she like? Is she pretty? Oh my God, where did you meet her?

jokes.text: Rachel tells the passenger she's 'going to London to tell this guy that I love him' — passenger goes completely silent, clearly horrified
jokes.setup: The passenger has demanded an explanation for Rachel's agitation
jokes.punchline: Rachel's explanation — going to tell a man she loves him at his wedding — provokes a reaction beat of horrified silence from the passenger, who clearly knows this is a terrible idea
jokes.explanation: The passenger's silent judgment (implied by the [whistling] sound effect immediately after and Rachel's obliviousness) is a good reaction beat. The humor comes from the gap between Rachel's romanticism and everyone else's reality-based horror.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Have you seen Monica?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica? No! Why would I have seen Monica? I haven't seen Monica. Monica and I haven't even been in the same room. Well, we have, but we weren't doing anything! I mean, there's nothing to see here!

jokes.text: Joey, told Rachel is coming to tell Ross she loves him, initially responds: 'Oh, great!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls to warn that Rachel is coming to London to ruin the wedding
jokes.punchline: Joey's instant reaction is enthusiastic excitement — until he processes that this is a problem
jokes.explanation: Joey's reflexive enthusiasm for all things Rachel before his brain catches up is very character-specific and gets a quick laugh. The beat between 'Oh, great!' and the correction is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So where is Monica?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's at work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: When will she be back?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Around 6.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What's she doing there?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Alright, we're gonna do this the hard way. You have the right to remain silent. Anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law.

jokes.text: After being told to stop Rachel, Joey immediately asks: 'Right. So tell me about this girl.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just given Joey an urgent mission to stop Rachel from ruining the wedding
jokes.punchline: Joey's first follow-up question is about the bridesmaid he hooked up with — completely ignoring the emergency
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey. He accepts the responsibility, says the right thing, and in the same breath completely drops it to pursue his love life. The pivot is abrupt and characterful. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to tell him. I'm going to tell him at his wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: That's the worst thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: When asked if he's seen Monica, Chandler blurts 'I'm not seeing Monica!'
jokes.setup: Joey asks where Monica is so they can warn her about Rachel
jokes.punchline: Chandler's defensive 'I'm not seeing Monica!' is a Freudian slip — far too emphatic a denial to be innocent, immediately exposing the hookup
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best gags. Chandler's over-defensive denial makes no sense in context (Joey asked 'Have you seen Monica?' not 'Are you in a relationship with Monica?') and the disproportion of the response is the joke. Perfect economy — four words reveal everything. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: That's a terrible plan.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: Phoebe thinks so too.

jokes.text: When Joey asks where Monica is, Chandler says 'No, okay? What's with the third degree? Why don't you just shine a light in my eyes?'
jokes.setup: Joey is asking simple questions about Monica's whereabouts
jokes.punchline: Chandler responds as though being interrogated by police — 'shine a light in my eyes' — over what is a completely innocent question
jokes.explanation: Chandler's escalating paranoia about simple questions is a good extension of the previous gag. 'Shine a light in my eyes' is a funny over-reaction that sells his guilt. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: You know, I've been married for thirty years. The secret is communication. You have to talk to each other.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's really sweet. Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Airplane Passenger
dialogue.line: Of course, my wife and I haven't spoken in twelve years, but that's beside the point.

jokes.text: On the plane, the passenger interrupts Rachel's revelation: 'Oh! Oh! Oh! I'm sorry. Can I interrupt? I just want to say that you are a horrible, horrible person.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been talking through her emotional journey and realizing she's been using other men as replacements for Ross
jokes.punchline: The passenger has been listening silently and can no longer contain herself — her interruption to call Rachel 'a horrible, horrible person' is blunt, funny, and completely accurate
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best laughs. The passenger has been silently judging Rachel for the whole flight and finally snaps. The double 'horrible, horrible person' is funny in its emphasis — she's not pulling punches. It's also genuinely correct, which makes it funnier. The polite 'I'm sorry, can I interrupt?' before the insult is a perfect British delivery setup.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I just hope our wedding looks as good as this.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm sure it will be great, but you know me, I'm probably going to say something stupid and ruin the whole—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Skip ahead.

jokes.text: The passenger: 'You're about to ruin the happiest day of his life.' Then adds: 'I have to agree with your friend Pheebs. This is a terrible, terrible plan.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has explained her plan to tell Ross she loves him at his wedding
jokes.punchline: The stranger not only agrees with Phoebe (a character she's never met) but has apparently fully absorbed Phoebe's nickname for Rachel
jokes.explanation: The stranger using 'Pheebs' — adopting the Friend group's nickname for a character she's heard Rachel reference — is a funny detail. The pattern of doubled adjectives ('terrible, terrible') mirrors the previous 'horrible, horrible' and creates a consistent voice for the passenger.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Monica, can you watch for Chandler?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't like the guy I just slept with.

jokes.text: The passenger delivers a verdict: 'By the way, it seems to be clear you were on a break.'
jokes.setup: The passenger has heard Rachel's whole story and is weighing in
jokes.punchline: She takes a side in the most famous ongoing Friends argument — 'they were on a break' — played as though it's a legal ruling from an impartial judge
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-line callbacks in Friends history. The passenger — a total stranger — has absorbed Rachel's backstory and delivers a ruling on the most contentious Ross/Rachel debate as though it's self-evident. The audience gasps/erupts because she's validating Ross's position. Perfect economy (one sentence), extremely high quotability, massive impact. The setup (Rachel's self-pitying narration) earns the punchline entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Fuggedaboutit! I'm walkin' here! Ey, what's up with you?

dialogue.speaker: Felicity
dialogue.line: Oh my god, that accent is so sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah? You want more? How ya doin'? Fuhgeddaboudit! I'm from New Yawk, baby!

jokes.text: Rachel gasps audibly at the 'you were on a break' verdict
jokes.setup: The passenger has just sided with Ross on the 'we were on a break' debate
jokes.punchline: Rachel's audible gasp is the audience surrogate reaction — but it's also funny because she can't argue with a stranger's impartial assessment
jokes.explanation: The gasp is a button to joke #51 and extends the laugh. Rachel being rendered speechless by a stranger's accurate assessment is funny in context even if the beat itself isn't independently crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Steven
dialogue.line: Can't we just meet in the middle on the wedding costs?

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: Meet in the middle? I'll meet you in the middle of the street and hit you with a car!

jokes.text: Monica and Emily's mutual reaction to the wedding venue: Monica: 'Oh, my God! It's like a fairyland.' Emily: 'I know. It's horrible, isn't it?' Monica: 'I love it.'
jokes.setup: Monica and Emily are looking at the wedding decorations
jokes.punchline: Emily says 'it's horrible, isn't it' and Monica immediately responds 'I love it' — they're in complete agreement that it's excessive and wonderful simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A quick, likable exchange. The rhythm of 'horrible, isn't it' / 'I love it' works as a compact bit of character bonding. Monica's wedding obsession is consistent characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mom, Dad, if you don't stop fighting, I'm not having kids. You'll never have grandchildren.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Geller
dialogue.line: You're not having kids anyway!

jokes.text: Monica: 'I only hope my wedding looks this good.' Emily's assistant tries to react; Monica says 'You can let some go by.'
jokes.setup: Monica is emotionally moved by the wedding decorations and daydreaming about her own wedding
jokes.punchline: 'You can let some go by' — Monica is so at ease with her own romantic desperation that she gives her companion permission to not react to every sad admission
jokes.explanation: An excellent self-aware Monica line. 'You can let some go by' acknowledges her own desperation with enough distance to be funny rather than tragic. Character integration is strong — Monica's self-aware neurosis is well-rendered.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, Steven. I shouldn't have said those things. Ross was right to call me out.

dialogue.speaker: Jack
dialogue.line: I apologize sincerely, and if you ever tell anyone about this, I will destroy you.

jokes.text: Joey gets a secret signal from Chandler and responds: 'I'll cover the door. You watch that big hole.' Then: 'I've got Chandler covering Ross.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to coordinate surveillance to intercept Rachel before she can reach Ross
jokes.punchline: Monica asks why she should care where Chandler is; Joey's casually mentions Chandler covering Ross as though it's a standard spy operation, while Monica gives away her interest in Chandler with 'Why would I care where Chandler is?'
jokes.explanation: Monica's over-casual 'Why would I care where Chandler is?' gives herself away. Decent cringe beat but not particularly well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: You can't see me before the wedding. It's bad luck!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily, come on. Bad luck? We've been through hell. We have real problems.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: I don't care. Superstition or not, I'm not taking any chances.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What could possibly be worse luck than what we've already had?

jokes.text: Monica: 'You know, uh... sometimes I don't even like Chandler.' Beat. Then walks away.
jokes.setup: Monica has accidentally revealed she cares about Chandler's location; she's trying to cover
jokes.punchline: 'Sometimes I don't even like Chandler' is such a transparently unconvincing lie, delivered so awkwardly, that it confirms everything
jokes.explanation: A perfectly chosen line. The awkward pause and transparent denial ('sometimes I don't even LIKE Chandler') is funnier because it's such a bad lie. The beat before she walks away is the visual punchline. Rewatch bonus for knowing what's happening.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, I need to tell you something. I love—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Congratulations.

jokes.text: Joey taking a phone call in the middle of the wedding ceremony while walking down the aisle: 'Hey, Felicity. Um, I thought about you all day.'
jokes.setup: The wedding ceremony is beginning and everyone is in position
jokes.punchline: Joey is chatting up his bridesmaid conquest on a cell phone while literally walking down the aisle as best man
jokes.explanation: Joey's inability to separate his romantic pursuits from any occasion — including being literally in the wedding procession — is excellent character comedy. The juxtaposition of solemn ceremony and flirty phone call is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I was so worried Rachel was going to do something to ruin the wedding, but everything went perfectly!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, nothing bad happened at all.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! I'm so relieved. What could possibly go wrong now?

jokes.text: Joey, still on phone mid-aisle: 'Talk New York to me again.' / 'Forget about it.' / 'How you doing?' — Felicity moans.
jokes.setup: Joey has charmed a British woman by speaking in New York slang/dialect
jokes.punchline: 'Talk New York to me again' — Joey has turned his New York accent into a seduction tool; his catchphrase 'How you doing?' produces an audible moan at a wedding
jokes.explanation: A legitimately great comedic construction. 'Talk New York to me' is a funny concept (treating a regional accent as verbal foreplay), and Joey's catchphrase 'How you doing?' producing a moan during a wedding ceremony is the perfect payoff. High character integration, strong concept originality, very quotable. The incongruity of location elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She's starting down the aisle now... Oh wow, that's a really long walk. Really long. I don't know if she's gonna make it. Her legs are moving but she's not getting any closer.

jokes.text: Steven's negotiating threat: 'My foot will meet the middle of your ass.'
jokes.setup: The fathers' negotiation over the wedding bill has escalated to open threats
jokes.punchline: Steven delivers a surprisingly specific and un-British threat that mirrors Jack's earlier aggression — revealing that both fathers are equally volatile
jokes.explanation: A decent escalation in the father-conflict subplot. 'The middle of your ass' is specific enough to be funny but it's not a particularly original insult.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hold on, Phoebe wants to listen.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Joey, we're in the middle of the ceremony!

jokes.text: Steven: 'You have to meet me in the middle.' Jack: 'My foot will meet the middle of your ass.'
jokes.setup: Steven appeals for a compromise on the financial dispute
jokes.punchline: Jack weaponizes Steven's own language ('meet in the middle') against him with a physical threat
jokes.explanation: Sharp wordplay. Taking 'meet in the middle' and redirecting it to a physical threat is a good setup/punchline structure. The economy is excellent — the wordplay does all the work. Very Jack Geller.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We said we weren't going to do this anymore. We called it stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, it is stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So we're not doing it again.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, we're not.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Never again.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Never.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay... so, same time next week?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, same time next week.

jokes.text: Ross breaks up the fathers' fight: 'Parents! Parents! Back away! This is our wedding day! From now on, everyone gets along. And if I hear one more word... no grandchildren!' — both couples immediately comply.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to stop the fathers from physically fighting at his wedding
jokes.punchline: 'No grandchildren!' — Ross's nuclear threat, withheld for maximum effect, instantly defuses a situation that physical demands couldn't. The parents' immediate compliance is the button.
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'no grandchildren' gambit is well-structured — it's his only real leverage over all four parents simultaneously, and it works immediately. The escalation to this nuclear option lands as a solid comedic beat. Well-paced, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I, Ross, take thee Rachel—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I, Ross, take thee Emily.

jokes.text: Steven says under breath: 'I could kill you with my thumb, you know.'
jokes.setup: Steven has just been forced to back down and apologize by Ross's grandchildren threat
jokes.punchline: His parting whispered threat — 'I could kill you with my thumb' — is so absurd and specific that it functions as a muttered protest rather than a credible threat
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the fathers' conflict. 'I could kill you with my thumb' is specific, absurd, and delivered as a save-face whisper. Very quotable. The thumb detail makes it funnier than a generic threat.

dialogue.speaker: Pastor
dialogue.line: Do you take this woman?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I do.

dialogue.speaker: Pastor
dialogue.line: Well, I'm sorry but I can't marry you.

jokes.text: Ross tells Emily not to worry about bad luck from seeing him before the wedding: 'I think we've had all the bad luck we're going to have.'
jokes.setup: Emily is worried about the bad luck of seeing Ross before the wedding
jokes.punchline: Ross reassures her that they've already exhausted their bad luck quota — which is darkly ironic given that he's about to say another woman's name at the altar
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony elevated to comedy. The audience knows what's coming; Ross doesn't. 'I think we've had all the bad luck we're going to have' is a brilliantly wrong statement. High rewatch value because it only fully lands when you know the ending.

jokes.text: Ross sees Rachel at the wedding and laughs with surprise: 'My God, Rachel! You're here. I can't believe it.' — His joy is oblivious to what she's actually there for.
jokes.setup: Rachel has arrived at the wedding to confess her love; we know this; Ross does not
jokes.punchline: Ross's pure delight at seeing his friend — 'my God, Rachel!' — is played completely straight but is funny through dramatic irony; she's there to ruin his wedding and he thinks it's a lovely surprise
jokes.explanation: More dramatic irony than outright comedy, but the audience's awareness of what Rachel is about to do makes Ross's enthusiasm funny. The tension is the joke.

jokes.text: Joey walking down the aisle during the actual ceremony while still on the phone with Phoebe, narrating events in real time: 'Still walking. Now I'm at the front with Ross. It's Phoebe!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has begged Joey to hold up the phone so she can listen to the ceremony
jokes.punchline: Joey is walking down the aisle providing live play-by-play commentary to Phoebe on his phone during the ceremony — including announcing 'It's Phoebe!' to Ross when she presumably says something
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully absurd sequence. Joey providing live wedding commentary while in the ceremony, then announcing 'It's Phoebe!' to Ross like a sportscaster calling in a substitution, is both very Joey and structurally inventive. The image of a best man on the phone at the altar is a great visual.

jokes.text: Post-ceremony morning-after beat: Monica and Chandler's friend is about to leave. Monica: 'What we did last night was—' Friend: 'Stupid.' Monica: 'Totally crazy, stupid.' Friend: 'What were we thinking?' Monica: 'I'm coming over tonight though, right?'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are mutually agreeing their hookup was a mistake
jokes.punchline: Even as they're agreeing it was 'crazy, stupid,' Monica immediately confirms she's coming over that night — completely undermining the regret
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured reversal. The setup is a mutual agreement it was a mistake; the punchline demolishes that agreement in the same breath with 'I'm coming over tonight though, right?' It signals the beginning of their relationship while being funny on its own. High rewatch value. One of the stronger comedic beats in the episode.

jokes.text: Ross says his vows: 'I, Ross. Take thee, Emily. Take thee, Rachel—'
jokes.setup: Ross is repeating his vows at the altar; the ceremony has been going smoothly
jokes.punchline: He says Rachel's name instead of Emily's — the single most catastrophic possible error at a wedding, played as a complete shock after a seemingly normal ceremony
jokes.explanation: The climactic joke of the episode and one of the most impactful single moments in the series. The entire episode has been structured to build to this — Rachel's near-confession, Ross's oblivious happiness, all the tension about whether Rachel would ruin it. When Ross says 'Rachel,' the room collapses. The structure is flawless: perfectly timed, maximum economy (one wrong word), and the character integration is as deep as it gets — it confirms what every viewer has always known about Ross. Stands as one of the defining comedic/dramatic moments of the series.

jokes.text: Emily shrieks: 'EMILY!'
jokes.setup: Ross has just said 'Rachel' in his wedding vows
jokes.punchline: Emily's one-word shriek of her own name is the button — both funny and devastating, the perfect reaction to being replaced in your own vows
jokes.explanation: Emily screaming her own name at her own wedding is the perfect button to the climax. It's both the funniest and most tragic reaction possible — she has to remind her groom who he's marrying. 'EMILY!' as a one-word punchline achieves maximum economy.

jokes.text: Ross's desperate correction: 'Ha. Emily.' Then crowd murmur.
jokes.setup: Ross has said Rachel's name; Emily has screamed her own name in correction
jokes.punchline: Ross's pathetic 'Ha. Emily.' — delivered with a nervous laugh and the word as though trying to pass it off as a slip — is one of the most cringe-inducing moments in the series
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'Ha. Emily.' is a masterwork of comedic delivery — the nervous laugh, the pause, the correction that changes nothing. It's the sound of a man trying to walk back the worst possible mistake. Perfect economy, strong character work. The crowd murmur as ambient soundtrack to the disaster completes the scene.

jokes.text: The minister turns to the crowd: 'Uh... Shall I go on?'
jokes.setup: The ceremony has just completely imploded; the crowd is murmuring in shock
jokes.punchline: The minister's dry, matter-of-fact 'Shall I go on?' treats an apocalyptic social disaster with professional bureaucratic detachment
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode and one of the best. 'Shall I go on?' is perfect deadpan understatement — the minister's professional neutrality in the face of complete chaos is both hilarious and brilliant. Maximum economy (four words), highly quotable, and it's the ideal note to end on. The ambiguity of whether to continue the ceremony mirrors the ambiguity of the entire Ross/Emily/Rachel triangle.

insight: Season finale abandons comedy for drama—lowest Friends humor score despite 62 jokes in play.
